clue.text: Consecutive communication between footballers?

blocks.note: first meaning: one straight after another, in an unbroken run
second, playful meaning: a pass from one defender to another defender on the same team

explanation.surface: A puzzle about how team-mates on the pitch talk to each other one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: In football the defenders are called backs, so a ball played from one of them to another goes back to back; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for things happening in unbroken succession, such as wins in consecutive matches.

clue.text: Mad scientist's away into asylum

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the word for away is placed within the asylum

blocks.note: off means away, as in going off
loony bin is slang for a mental asylum

explanation.surface: A crazed researcher has escaped into the madhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Boffin is British slang for a scientist or researcher, often pictured as eccentric, which is what lets 'Mad' sit in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A boffin is the British colloquial word for a scientist, typically imagined as an absent-minded, eccentric technical expert.

clue.text: Study includes source of light and source of shade

indicators.note: a word that includes something holds it inside

blocks.note: to con is an old word for to study or learn
a ray is a beam coming from a lamp or the sun

explanation.surface: A room with a lamp and somewhere to sit out of the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: Shade means a colour or shading on paper, not shelter from the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: A crayon is a stick of coloured wax used for drawing, which supplies colours and shading to a picture.

clue.text: Ornate blurb all set to capture first appearance of unique rock album

indicators.note: the first appearance of a word is its opening letter
capturing something takes it inside, so a letter joins the jumble
ornate suggests elaborately worked, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
the opening letter of unique

explanation.surface: Flowery sleeve notes ready to describe an extraordinary new rock record.
explanation.definitionFit: Tubular Bells is the 1973 debut album by the English musician Mike Oldfield, a landmark of progressive rock.

clue.text: Purchases extra items in the audio department?

indicators.note: the audio department deals in sound, so the word is taken by how it sounds

blocks.note: byes are extras in cricket, runs scored without the bat touching the ball

explanation.surface: Shoppers in the hi-fi section of a store pick up some extras.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bye is a run that counts as an extra, conceded when the ball passes the batter and the keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Buys are things bought, so as a noun the word means purchases.

clue.text: French composer unable to compose, having lost heart, unfortunately

indicators.note: losing its heart means the inside of the word goes, leaving only its edges
things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
only the outside letters are kept

explanation.surface: A French composer with writer's block, dispirited and down on his luck.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart lost here is the whole middle of 'compose', not just one letter, a loose use. Joseph Canteloube is known for his Songs of the Auvergne.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Canteloube was a French composer famous for arranging the folk songs of the Auvergne region.

clue.text: Religious follower taken aback by some French kissing

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are wanted, a run lying inside them
taken aback suggests being pulled backwards, so the run is read from right to left

blocks.note: a run straddling the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A devout believer is startled by a Gallic snog.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sikh is an adherent of Sikhism, the faith founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab.

clue.text: One broken latrine, showing unwillingness to shift?

indicators.note: something broken is smashed up, so its letters are put back together differently

blocks.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A blocked toilet that will not budge.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a physics term: inertia is a body's resistance to changing its motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertial describes inertia, the tendency of a body at rest to resist being moved.

clue.text: Hard drink, unknown booze, not entirely a stinger?

indicators.note: not entirely means not the whole thing, so the drink loses its last letter

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
a drink, as in having a quick one
y is a mathematical unknown
beer is an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: A bar order of a strong drink and a mystery spirit, almost a Stinger cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: A Stinger is a brandy cocktail, which the drinks in the surface point towards; the question mark says the answer is a creature that stings.
explanation.definitionFit: A honeybee can sting, so it is a stinger in the literal sense of an insect armed with a sting.

clue.text: Outrageous fellow imprisoning lad in apartment

indicators.note: to imprison is to shut something inside, so the fellow surrounds the lad
the combination is placed inside the apartment's letters

blocks.note: a flat is a British apartment
a fellow is a man
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A scandalous man has locked a youngster in his flat.
explanation.walkthrough: A nested container: the lad goes inside the fellow first, and only then does that combined chunk go inside the apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamboyant behaviour or dress is showy and extravagant, which is what outrageous means of a person's style.

clue.text: What contains claret or plonk that English'll tuck into

indicators.note: to tuck one thing into another is to put it inside, so English goes within the wine

blocks.note: plonk is cheap wine, VIN in French
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Talk of a wine bottle, of claret or plonk, that an Englishman will happily knock back.
explanation.walkthrough: Claret is old slang for blood, so the definition is a blood vessel, not a bottle; 'that' points back to the plonk the E tucks into.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood flows through veins, and claret is a slang term for blood from boxing commentary.

clue.text: Triangle blended with piano? It's hardly this!

indicators.note: things blended are mixed up together, so the letters are combined in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
p is the musical marking for piano, softly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A quiet triangle mixed with a softly played piano is hardly deafening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' does double duty: its letters join the jumble, and 'hardly this' says that a quiet, piano sound is anything but the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ear-splitting means extremely loud, the opposite of piano, the musical term for playing softly.

clue.text: I wish one pilot to carry on

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it within, so the flying word holds the next word

blocks.note: one is the Roman numeral I
to pilot an aircraft is to fly it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a single aviator to keep going.
explanation.walkthrough: Pilot looks like a noun, a flyer, but it is the verb meaning to steer an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase expresses a wish or regret about something that is not so, exactly like saying I wish.

clue.text: Soldier engaging in exercises with dull precision

indicators.note: to engage in something is to be involved within it, so the soldier sits inside the other pieces

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school exercises
dull, uninteresting writing is dry
a soldier is a caste of ant, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A soldier going through drill with tedious exactness.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldier is not a military abbreviation here but the soldier caste of insect, a favourite crossword device.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedantry is excessive concern with minor details and correctness, fussy exactness taken too far.

clue.text: Ballerina in troupe tries endless spinning

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the last letter is dropped
spinning things turn and tumble, so the letters are whirled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer in a ballet company keeps attempting turns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spinning' fits the dancer so well that it hides its job of stirring the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballerina regularly performs pirouettes, full turns on one foot, so she is a pirouetter.

clue.text: Rebellious agitator tries releasing one from entry to prison

indicators.note: releasing a prisoner lets them out, so one letter is let out of the word it follows
rebellious letters refuse to stay in order and are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I, the letter released

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser seeks a jailbreak, trying to get someone out from the moment they go inside.
explanation.walkthrough: Traitors' Gate is the river entrance to the Tower of London, through which prisoners were brought in by boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Traitors' Gate is the historic water gate by which accused prisoners entered the Tower of London to be locked up.

clue.text: Accountants targeted rising universities

indicators.note: in a down clue rising letters read upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.note: an ACA is an Associate of the Institute of Chartered Accountants
to target is to aim at

explanation.surface: Bean-counters have their sights on colleges whose fortunes are improving.
explanation.definitionFit: Academia is the world of higher education and scholarship, the collective realm of colleges and their scholars.

clue.text: Mountain feature beginning to seduce one bird in nine

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
the bird is placed inside the number

blocks.note: the opening letter of seduce
taken as written
an owl is a single bird

explanation.surface: On a mountain, a would-be seducer picks out one bird from a group of nine.
explanation.definitionFit: The snowline is the altitude on a mountain above which snow lies all year round.

clue.text: Clever boy, not working – one should provide continuous supply

indicators.note: working letters are being worked over and shaped into something new

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bright lad who is idle when he ought to be keeping things coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not working' reads as one idea, idle, but it splits: NOT joins the fodder and 'working' stirs it.
explanation.definitionFit: A conveyor belt is a moving band that carries goods along a factory line in an unending stream.

clue.text: Impulse for business proposal limited by rising fuel

indicators.note: in a down clue rising letters read from the bottom up
something limited by another thing is bounded on both sides by it

blocks.note: oil is a fuel
a bid is an offer made in business

explanation.surface: The drive behind a company's offer is constrained by climbing fuel prices.
explanation.definitionFit: Libido is the psychological drive or urge, especially sexual desire, the energy behind instinctive behaviour.

clue.text: City, one on bearing to south

blocks.note: a means one
mien is a person's bearing or manner
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Navigating to a city by taking a compass bearing southwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Bearing looks like a compass direction, which 'south' reinforces; here it is a person's demeanour.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiens is a cathedral city in northern France, the capital of Picardy on the River Somme.

clue.text: Pinned hoax on feeble type penning lines

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so the feeble type encloses the lines

blocks.note: to do someone is to cheat or hoax them
a weed is a weak, puny person
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for lines

explanation.surface: A prank played on a weakling who is writing lines as a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: A dowel is a wooden peg used to join two pieces of wood, so dowelled means fixed with such pegs.
explanation.definitionFit: Joinery pieces that are dowelled are fastened together with wooden pins pushed into matching holes.

clue.text: University investing in a well-organised entrance hall

indicators.note: to invest is to clothe or surround, read here as going inside what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
trim means neat and in good order
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A college puts money into a smartly laid-out lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: Investing looks financial; here it means putting U inside TRIM, after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrium is the open central hall at the entrance of a large building, originally of a Roman house.

clue.text: Fellow's inferior legislation, showing an error

indicators.note: inferior literally means lower down, so in a down clue this piece sits beneath the fellow

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
a law is a piece of legislation

explanation.surface: A man's shoddy statute turns out to be a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: Inferior looks like a judgement of quality, but in a down clue it means placed underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A flaw is a fault or mistake in something, a defect that spoils it.

clue.text: Correspondence – African country rejecting half

indicators.note: rejecting something turns it away, and only half of the country's name is turned round

blocks.note: Mali is a country in West Africa

explanation.surface: Letters exchanged with an African nation that turns down half of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second half of the country's name, LI, is turned round; the MA stays put.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail is the letters and parcels sent by post, which is what correspondence means collectively.

clue.text: Eavesdrop, being quiet – that is, restraining detectives

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold back within limits, so the detectives are held inside

blocks.note: to be still is to be silent and motionless
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

explanation.surface: Listen in secretly while keeping silent, which means holding back the police.
explanation.walkthrough: Eavesdrop wants to be the verb to listen in; read it as eaves-drop, water dripping from the eaves of a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Stillicide is a rare word for a dripping of water, especially rainwater falling drop by drop from the edge of a roof.

clue.text: Top copy given a critical mark

blocks.note: to ape someone is to imitate them
a cross marks a wrong answer, a critical mark

explanation.surface: The best copy of a document gets marked down by a reviewer.
explanation.definitionFit: The apex is the highest point or peak of something, its very summit.

clue.text: PM's securing quality audio equipment

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it firmly in place, here within the other word

blocks.note: Gordon Brown was Prime Minister when the puzzle appeared, plus the possessive S
good as a noun is a desirable quality

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister is buying top-grade hi-fi kit.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown goods is the retail trade's name for televisions and hi-fi, once encased in brown wood, as opposed to white goods such as fridges.
explanation.definitionFit: Retailers use the category name for home electronics such as stereos, radios and televisions.
